titleEn: Eleven-Year-Old Struck in the Chest by a Baseball - Commotio Cordis

patient.name: Caleb Mercer
patient.affectEn: In cardiac arrest on arrival: motionless on his back on the firm infield dirt, jersey pulled open, skin pale grey, only an occasional slow gasp; the chest moves with the coach's compressions. After ROSC he stays unresponsive (GCS 8, later 9) with slow, shallow, irregular breathing that needs BVM assistance.
patient.speechEn: No speech at any point - he is unresponsive throughout. History comes from his coach, who saw the collapse, and from his mother, who arrives during care.

scene.settingEn: Community ballpark in Langley at 1841 hrs, a dry sunny evening. The infield is firm packed dirt and the teammates have been moved to the dugout. A boy lies on his back near third base with his jersey pulled open; his coach kneels beside him giving chest compressions and a parent is on the phone with the dispatcher. The baseball lies nearby. There is no AED at the park. One patient, no hazards. The hospital is 14 minutes away. Fire First Responders are not currently assigned; if the candidate asks, dispatch will send them.
hazardsEn: none - firm infield dirt, teammates moved to the dugout

bystanders.knowsEn: A ground ball took a bad hop and hit the boy squarely in the left chest during infield practice at about 1833, about 8 minutes before your arrival. He put a hand to his chest, took a step and dropped, and never spoke again. No head strike, no fall from a height. The coach started compressions within about a minute, the emergency call was made at once, no AED was available and no shock has been given. He keeps compressing until the candidate tells him to stop, and follows instructions exactly.

bystanders.who: parent on the phone with the dispatcher
bystanders.knowsEn: Called 911 and is still on the line. Saw the ball hit him in the chest. Knows nothing more about his history. Will open the gate, guide the crew or keep the crowd back if asked.

His weight is about 32 kg. He is a healthy boy: no heart condition, no fainting or chest pain with exercise, no family history of sudden death. No prescription medications. No known allergies. Last ate a sandwich at about 1700 and had a sports drink at practice. She answers the Functional Enquiry for him and can ride along.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: AED with adult and child (paediatric) pads
BVM with oxygen reservoir and tubing
BP cuffs in child and adult sizes and a stethoscope
PCP only: supraglottic airway and IV start kit

dispatchEn: 1834 hrs. Code 3 to a community ballpark in Langley. 11-year-old male was struck in the chest by a baseball, collapsed and is not breathing. The coach is doing CPR. Hospital is 14 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch update en route: the caller (a parent) says the boy was hit in the chest by a ground ball, dropped at once and has not moved or breathed normally since; the coach started compressions about a minute later. There is no AED at the park. Fire First Responders are not currently assigned.
arrivalEn: A dry, sunny evening at the ballpark. A boy lies on his back near third base with his jersey pulled open; his coach kneels beside him giving chest compressions and a parent is on the phone with the dispatcher. The infield is firm packed dirt and the teammates have been moved to the dugout. Bystanders say a ground ball hit him in the chest. The baseball lies nearby. There is no AED at the park. One patient, no hazards.
firstLookEn: A boy lying supine and motionless on the firm infield dirt near third base, jersey pulled open. His coach kneels beside him giving chest compressions and a parent is on the phone with the dispatcher.

primary.locEn: Unresponsive: no response to voice and no response to a painful stimulus (AVPU = U).
primary.airwayEn: Closed by the tongue; it opens with a manual maneuver. No vomit, fluid or foreign object.
primary.breathingEn: DURING THE ARREST: no breathing, only an occasional slow gasp (agonal) when compressions pause for the check - not effective breathing; the chest rises equally with ventilation. SpO2 cannot be read (no pulse). AFTER ROSC: respirations 10 per minute, shallow and irregular - the breathing must still be assisted with the BVM.
primary.circulationEn: DURING THE ARREST: no brachial or carotid pulse within 10 seconds of checking breathing and pulse together; no external bleeding. Every pulse check before the engine announces signs of life finds NO pulse. AED (give the device prompt only when the candidate turns it on and lets it analyze): first analysis - "Shock advised"; second analysis, after 2 minutes of CPR - "Shock advised". If the candidate places the adult pads in the standard anterior/lateral position on his small chest, they sit about 2 cm apart, within 2.5 cm of each other. AFTER the engine announces signs of life (ROSC): a pulse check finds a pulse of 126, regular, with a weak radial pulse. Any analysis after ROSC - "No shock advised".
primary.rbsEn: Chest exposed during CPR: round red bruise over the left lower chest where the ball hit, no open wound, no deformity, the chest rises equally with ventilation. No head injury, no bleeding, no other injuries. Skin pale grey, cool and dry, lips blue (skin is given automatically during the RBS).
primary.skinEn: pale grey, cool and dry, with blue lips

expected.actionEn: Recognize from dispatch that a witnessed collapse after a blow to the chest is a sudden rhythm arrest (commotio cordis, likely shockable) - AED first, not an asphyxial arrest
triggers: witnessed collapse after a chest blow

expected.actionEn: Consider additional resources (First Responders) to relieve the compressors and support the family
triggers: get fire to relieve the compressors

expected.actionEn: Anticipate an outdoor field with an upset crowd; PPE incl gloves and eye protection
Verbalize hazards (none), environment (outdoor field, firm ground), mechanism (baseball to the chest) and number of patients (1)
triggers: mechanism is a baseball to the chest

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection
triggers: putting on gloves and eye protection

expected.actionEn: First look: boy supine and motionless, coach doing compressions, parent on the phone - treat as cardiac arrest until proven otherwise
triggers: treating this as a cardiac arrest

expected.actionEn: Keep the coach compressing without a pause (interruptions under 5 seconds) while the AED, BVM and oxygen are brought in; request First Responders
triggers: continue compressions while we set up

expected.actionEn: Assess LOC / AVPU: Unresponsive (U) - no response to voice or pain
triggers: no response to voice or pain

expected.actionEn: Verbalize c-spine not indicated: witnessed collapse after a chest blow, no head or neck impact, no fall - spinal trauma can be reasonably ruled out, so CPR and the AED are not delayed
Assess airway: open it with a manual maneuver and look for vomit, fluid or a foreign object - clear
Assess breathing: none; an occasional gasp is not breathing - start ventilations
triggers: look listen and feel for breathing

expected.actionEn: Check breathing and pulse together for no more than 10 seconds (brachial, or carotid); no pulse = cardiac arrest, so CPR continues
Expose the chest and do the rapid body survey during CPR without stopping compressions: find the ball-impact bruise, no open chest wound or other injury
Note skin: pale grey, cool, dry, cyanotic lips
Oxygen: connect the BVM to high-flow oxygen (15 L/min); SpO2 cannot be read in arrest
Position: keep him supine on the firm ground for compressions; do not move him (move only for a dangerous scene or if CPR cannot be done effectively)
triggers: flat on the ground for compressions

expected.actionEn: Categorize as RTC (cardiac arrest, unconscious with no pulse) and act with urgency
Resuscitate where he lies and do not package or move him mid-cycle; load as soon as ROSC is confirmed
triggers: load as soon as we have ROSC

expected.actionEn: Ready to load within 15 minutes of arrival, with the secondary survey left for en route
Delegate effectively: partner takes over compressions, then brings the stretcher; a bystander opens the gate and guides the crew; a parent stays ready to give history and ride along
triggers: a parent stays to give history and ride along

expected.actionEn: Establish chief complaint: collapsed and stopped breathing after being hit in the chest by a baseball (cardiac arrest)
HxC/C from the coach: mechanism and point of impact, time of collapse, immediate collapse without warning, no head strike, when CPR started, no AED or shock before arrival
triggers: where did the ball hit him

triggers: does he have a heart problem

Apply the AED and analyse as soon as possible: a witnessed sudden collapse after a chest blow is a rhythm arrest, not an asphyxial arrest, so NO 5 cycles of CPR first (compressions continue while the pads go on)
triggers: AED analyze as soon as possible

expected.actionEn: CPR quality: interruptions under 5 seconds, rate 100-120 per minute, depth one third to one half of the chest diameter, full recoil, change the compressor every 2 minutes
triggers: one third to one half the chest depth

expected.actionEn: Two rescuers: ratio 15:2 with the BVM and oxygen, ventilating without hyperventilation
Pads: state the age rule (child pads are for 0-8 years, he is 11, so adult pads) and, with the pads within 2.5 cm of each other on his small chest, shift to anterior/posterior
triggers: pads are too close so anterior posterior
shift the pads to anterior posterior

expected.actionEn: Shock advised: deliver the shock, resume CPR at once, 2 minutes of CPR, analyse and repeat - second shock at the second analysis
triggers: resume CPR immediately after the shock
two minutes of CPR then analyze

expected.actionEn: Stop compressions at signs of ROSC (spontaneous breath, cough, eyelid movement), confirm the pulse, and never compress a patient who has a pulse
After ROSC suction the mouth for no more than 10 seconds (paediatric limit) and maintain the airway
triggers: suction for no more than 10 seconds

expected.actionEn: Assist his slow, shallow breathing with the BVM and oxygen at a controlled rate, avoid hyperventilation, titrate to SpO2 of 94% or more
triggers: assist his breathing with the BVM

expected.actionEn: Verbalize no analgesia: pain cannot be assessed and altered LOC contraindicates Entonox (the oral drugs need a patient who can swallow)
Reassess ABCs and all interventions after ROSC, after loading and after each move
triggers: recheck the airway and the BVM

expected.actionEn: Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes of the first and interpret the improving trend
Verbalize the re-arrest plan: if the pulse is lost, resume CPR at once and re-analyse with the AED
Re-check the airway for secretions and keep SpO2 at 94% or more at every reassessment
En-route notification for a critical patient (paediatric cardiac arrest with ROSC)
Complete hand-off: mechanism, age and weight, witnessed collapse, bystander CPR, shocks, ROSC, current vitals and response
State the times: collapse, CPR start, arrival, each shock and ROSC
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes with the shock times, ROSC time and the reason no analgesia was given

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate turns on the AED / attaches the pads and has it analyze the rhythm (personally or by delegating)

candidate says they will give 5 cycles / about 2 minutes of CPR before applying the AED, waits for the AED, First Responders or more help before the pads go on, or treats this as an asphyxial arrest. Applying the AED at once, or saying there is no need for 5 cycles first, is NOT this event.
the SECOND AED shock of this call is delivered (by the candidate or on their instruction). Record it only for the second shock - not for the first shock and not for an analysis without a shock
candidate treats the occasional gasping (agonal) breaths as breathing - e.g. says he is breathing, puts him in the recovery position, or does not start or continue CPR because of them

AFTER the examiner has described signs of life (coughing, a spontaneous breath, eyelids fluttering), the candidate continues or restarts chest compressions in a later line without first checking for a pulse, or continues compressions after a pulse has been found. Never record this for the candidate line that the signs-of-life description was answering. Stopping compressions and checking the pulse is NOT this event.
candidate stops compressions, or has everyone stand clear / hands off, while the AED is CHARGING (hands-off is correct only for the analysis and for the shock itself)

candidate stops compressions for more than about 5 seconds for anything other than the analysis and the shock - to place the pads, connect oxygen, suction, insert an airway, take vital signs, examine him, move him onto the stretcher or take over slowly - or stops them for a pulse / breathing check that lasts longer than 10 seconds
candidate has the compressor changed (the partner, the coach or another rescuer takes over compressions) as the 2-minute rotation

candidate states or directs 30 compressions to 2 ventilations (30:2) once two rescuers are doing CPR on this child (the child two-rescuer ratio is 15:2). Using 30:2 while a single rescuer is compressing, before the partner is in position, is NOT this event.
candidate chooses child / paediatric pads for this 11-year-old (child pads are for 0-8 years), or picks the pad size by his size or weight instead of his age. Choosing adult pads is NOT this event.
candidate places or shifts the AED pads to the anterior/posterior (front and back) position because the pads would sit too close together on his small chest
candidate delays the first ventilations (or the compressions) to connect oxygen to the BVM first
candidate verbalizes checking for or seeing chest rise with the BVM ventilations (or another sign that the ventilations are effective)
candidate ventilates at a clearly excessive rate at any point (rapid continuous squeezing of the bag, a breath every second or two)

after ROSC, while the latest reading the examiner gave still shows his own breathing slow, shallow and irregular (respirations 10), the candidate stops assisting with the BVM or switches him to a non-rebreather, nasal cannula, blow-by or no oxygen device. Switching to a non-rebreather AFTER a reading shows regular, adequate breathing (respirations 16) is NOT this event.
candidate suctions for longer than 10 seconds, or states a suction time longer than 10 seconds (the paediatric limit)
candidate stops or delays CPR, the pads or the AED to hold his head, apply a collar, board him or otherwise do spinal precautions. Saying that c-spine is not indicated is NOT this event.
an EMR-level candidate actually inserts a supraglottic airway or starts an IV (PCP skills). Saying these are PCP skills, or that the PCP will do them, is NOT this event.

PCP candidate stops or delays compressions or the AED sequence to insert a supraglottic airway or start an IV before high-quality CPR and the AED are established, or delays loading after ROSC to do either
after ROSC, candidate delays loading to complete the full head-to-toe, the Functional Enquiry, repeat vital signs or other non-priority tasks on scene instead of loading first and doing them en route

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR: CPR, AED, BVM with oxygen, suction, the pad and ratio rules and the 15-minute RTC clock are all EMR-level skills - this call is the same at EMR level. No Functional Enquiry (PCP only). No analgesia (altered LOC contraindicates Entonox; the oral analgesics are within EMR scope but he cannot swallow safely - textbook reasoning, not a monograph line). (Textbook practice - not a BC rubric item: leave the AED pads on after ROSC in case the rhythm refibrillates.)
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry en route (the mother answers). The guideline mentions supraglottic airway insertion for PCPs once high-quality arrest management is under way (p.42) - not needed here, because ROSC follows the second shock and BVM ventilation works. No protocol in the guideline calls for IV access, a fluid bolus or a drug in this post-ROSC child (BP is not below 90, no hypovolemia), so nothing else is added at PCP level - do not delay loading for vascular access.

sourcePages: Scenario md-12 (data/practical/scenarios-2.json): dispatch, scene, primary (unresponsive, gasps only, pulseless, ball-impact bruise), transport (RTC, resuscitate where he lies, load after ROSC), history (coach and mother), vitals sets 1-2 (post-ROSC), FE, exam, interventions (AED at once, pads, shocks, ROSC, suction, assisted ventilation, no analgesia), ongoing, handoff. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (cardiac arrest); p.9-10 Patient Assessment Model; p.11 primary-survey interventions (airway maintenance and suctioning, assisting inadequate respirations, CPR); p.13 AVPU; p.40-41 Adult and Child/Infant CPR/AED (assess breathing and pulse together for no more than 10 seconds; 15:2 with two rescuers; analyze as soon as possible); p.42 CPR/AED basic concepts (interruptions under 5 seconds, change operators every 2 minutes, ROSC signs, CPR more effective while stationary, SGA for PCPs); p.43-44 Infant/Child CPR/AED basics (100-120 per minute, 1/3 to 1/2 chest diameter, child pads for 0-8 years, pads within 2.5 cm shift to anterior/posterior) and Child Sudden Cardiac Arrest (commotio cordis); asphyxia arrest 5 cycles; p.45 suction 10 seconds in the paediatric patient; p.50 Oxygen Administration; p.57 Diabetic Emergencies (BGL with decreased LOC); p.58 Acetaminophen; p.65 Entonox (contraindication altered level of consciousness); p.68 Ibuprofen. Grading criteria p.19 (packaging goal times, cardiac arrest from ROSC), p.35 (vitals intervals).
